pr.title: Make the analyzer work when SuppressSourceGeneration = true (REQ-2234)
pr.body:
Requirement: REQ-2234

Agent-written implementation of requirement REQ-2234 (upstream MessagePack-CSharp issue 2234), from the Junction 2026 challenge branch `ju26-issue-2234`.

Author: coding agent. Accountable owner: to be assigned by Countersign.
pr.author: ToukoUrsin

requirement.title: The analyzer does not work if SuppressSourceGeneration = true
requirement.body:
#### Bug description

The analyzer does not work if SuppressSourceGeneration = true. This has happened since version 3.1.1. It still worked in 3.1.0.

criteria.text: When a type has SuppressSourceGeneration = true, the analyzer still reports the diagnostics it would report for the same type without that setting.
criteria.sourceQuote: The analyzer does not work if SuppressSourceGeneration = true.
criteria.note: Runs the analyzer on two types with the same rule-breaking body (a duplicate int key, a string key mixed with int keys, a member with no key), one plain and one with SuppressSourceGeneration = true, and expects the same MsgPack005/MsgPack005/MsgPack004 diagnostics on both and no AD0001.

criteria.text: A test exists that puts SuppressSourceGeneration = true on code that breaks an analyzer rule, and it fails before the fix and passes after it.
criteria.sourceQuote: The analyzer does not work if SuppressSourceGeneration = true.
criteria.note: Runs the MsgPack00x analyzer on a [MessagePackObject(SuppressSourceGeneration = true)] type with two [Key(0)] members and expects exactly one MsgPack005 on the second member and no analyzer exception (AD0001). Contested by FN2 (verified in code): the tests that pass do not cover that case.

criteria.text: For the same input that sets SuppressSourceGeneration = true, the analyzer reports the same diagnostics it reported in version 3.1.0.
criteria.sourceQuote: This has happened since version 3.1.1. It still worked in 3.1.0.
criteria.note: Supported by the PR author’s own tests (which do fail without the change), not by an independent probe. Contested by FN2 (verified in code): the tests that pass do not cover that case.

criteria.text: With SuppressSourceGeneration = true, no source is generated for the affected type, even though analyzer diagnostics are now reported.
criteria.note: Runs MessagePackGenerator through CSharpGeneratorDriver on a normal type and a SuppressSourceGeneration = true type, asserts the generator throws no exception, a NormalThing formatter is generated, and no generated file name or text refers to a SuppressedThing formatter.

criteria.text: Diagnostics for types that do not set SuppressSourceGeneration are unchanged, and all existing analyzer and source generator tests still pass.
criteria.note: Runs the analyzer on a valid non-suppressed type (expects no diagnostics), a non-suppressed type with a member missing its key (expects MsgPack004 only), and a valid suppressed type (expects no diagnostics).

story.headline: TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo no longer throws on duplicate [Key] values, so the analyzer can keep running and report its diagnostics instead of crashing.
story.before: For a [MessagePackObject] type with two members sharing a [Key] value, TypeCollector called Dictionary.Add a second time with the same key. That threw ArgumentException and aborted the analyzer run, so diagnostics such as MsgPack004/005 were not reported. The requirement describes this for types marked SuppressSourceGeneration = true.
story.after: In both member loops, a member is added to intMembers/stringMembers only if its key is not already there. The first member with a key wins, and MsgPack015 (KeysMustBeUnique) is still reported for the duplicate. A member whose key kind does not match the others is skipped after MsgPack005 is reported. None of the code checks SuppressSourceGeneration, so the change applies to every type.

steps.text: Both member-collection loops in GetObjectInfo (properties and fields) check ContainsKey before calling Add, for int keys and for string keys. The duplicate is reported and then dropped instead of throwing.
When a member's key kind differs from the first keyed member, the loop reports DoNotMixStringAndIntKeys (MsgPack005) and `continue`s, so the member is never processed further.
Analyzer tests run types marked SuppressSourceGeneration with duplicate int/string keys and with mixed key kinds. They expect MsgPack004/015/003/005 to be reported and MsgPack011/016/017 not to be.
Execution tests check that GeneratedMessagePackResolver returns no formatter for a suppressed type and that the type round-trips through the standard dynamic resolver.
A new README section explains SuppressSourceGeneration and lists which analyzer diagnostics still apply to it and which do not.

alsoTouches: The source generator calls the same TypeCollector.Collect path, so for non-suppressed types with duplicate keys it now produces a model that has only the first member per key, where before the collector threw.
Members whose key kind conflicts are now left out of the collected members for all types, not only for suppressed ones.
For a member skipped because of a mixed key kind, no checks that ran later in the loop body (for example formatter-attribute and key-validity checks) run on it any more.
The README now documents which diagnostics apply when source generation is suppressed.

diagrams.title: Duplicate/mixed-key handling in TypeCollector and who sees it
diagrams.caption: The fix lives in the shared GetObjectInfo, so the analyzer and the source generator both get the new skip-instead-of-throw behaviour, and neither path checks SuppressSourceGeneration.

diagrams.title: Analyzing a SuppressSourceGeneration type with duplicate keys
diagrams.caption: Before, the second Dictionary.Add threw and the analyzer stopped. Now the duplicate is reported and skipped, and analysis finishes.

units.title: Skip duplicate-key members instead of throwing in GetObjectInfo
units.summary: In both member-collection loops of TypeCollector, intMembers/stringMembers are now only added if the key is not already present, so duplicate [Key] values no longer throw ArgumentException from Dictionary.Add (which aborted the analyzer). The first member with a given key wins.

hunks.header: @@ -1617,6 +1617,20 @@ This code generation has a minor upfront performance cost.

lines.s: > Note: When using Unity, dynamic code generation only works when targeting .NET Framework 4.x + mono runtime.
For all other Unity targets, AOT is required.
A `[MessagePackObject]` type can opt out of source generation with `[MessagePackObject(SuppressSourceGeneration = true)]`.
No formatter is generated for that type. It is serialized at run time by the dynamic resolvers, which use reflection, so such a type is not AOT-safe.
The analyzer still validates these types, because they are serialized at run time and must still have a valid contract:
- Keys are unique and all of the same kind ([MsgPack005](doc/analyzers/MsgPack005.md)).
- Members have types that are themselves serializable ([MsgPack003](doc/analyzers/MsgPack003.md)).
- Types are accessible to the resolver ([MsgPack012](doc/analyzers/MsgPack012.md)).

The analyzer does not report the partial-class requirement ([MsgPack011](doc/analyzers/MsgPack011.md)) or the AOT-only checks ([MsgPack016](doc/analyzers/MsgPack016.md) and [MsgPack017](doc/analyzers/MsgPack017.md)) for these types, because they only apply when a formatter is generated.
You can customize the generated source through properties on the `GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute`.
continue; // The key kind does not match the other members; the diagnostic is reported, so skip this member.

evidence.title: Cross-checked: No hunk depends on SuppressSourceGeneration; fix targets a g
evidence.conclusion: The cited code exists verbatim in the PR head, and a second agent instructed to refute the finding could not. I read the diff. The only source changes are in TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo: Dictionary.Add is now guarded by ContainsKey on duplicate int/string keys, and a `continue` follows the DoNotMixStringAndIntKeys report. None of the changed lines reads suppressSourceGeneration; the variable is used only at lines 710, 921-947, 989, 1078-1101 and 1383, all unchanged. The crash this fixes (MsgPack005 reported, then Dictionary.Add throws) hit every [MessagePackObject] type before the PR, as the PR's own ...ForGeneratedTypes test shows. Four of the new tests (MsgPack004 at 921-933, MsgPack015 at 1366-1378, MsgPack003 at line 1359 via the recursive collect, and the suppressed-type guards plus the 1383 return) run through unchanged code, so by reading they pass with or without the fix. Without the issue text I can't tell whether the reporter's case was duplicate or mixed keys, so the PR doesn't show a link to a SuppressSourceGeneration-specific 3.1.1 regression. The crash itself is older than this PR; the scope gap between the requirement and the change comes from the PR.

evidence.title: Reviewer self-test: GPT-planted bugs
evidence.conclusion: 6 bugs were planted by GPT (2 single-line, 2 multi-line, 2 cross-file). The blind reviewer caught 4; the PR tests caught 5. A reviewer miss is counted even when a PR test catches it. Units containing reviewer misses are escalated to a human read. 6 candidate mutation(s) were discarded or did not compile.

findings.title: The PR's tests pass without the change
findings.body: The PR's tests pass with AND without the source change (2 pass on base). They do not demonstrate that the change does anything.

findings.title: No hunk depends on SuppressSourceGeneration; fix targets a generic duplicate/mixed-key throw
findings.body: The only production changes stop GetObjectInfo throwing on duplicate keys or mixed key kinds. None of them reads suppressSourceGeneration, and the PR's own DuplicateKeysAreReportedWithoutAnalyzerFailureForGeneratedTypes test shows the same change applies to plain [MessagePackObject] types. The suppress early-return sits after every diagnostic the new tests assert and is untouched. Four of the eight new analyzer tests (missing key, AllowPrivate, member type, generation-only diagnostics) exercise paths no hunk changes, so they cannot fail before the fix. The link to a 3.1.1 regression specific to SuppressSourceGeneration (AC2, AC3) is therefore not shown by this PR.
findings.scenario: Revert all of F2 and run MemberWithoutKeyIsReported, AllowPrivateRequiredIsReported, MemberTypeMustBeMessagePackObjectIsReported and SourceGenerationOnlyDiagnosticsAreNotReportedWhenSuppressed: by reading, the result is identical, because MsgPack004 (lines 913-933), MsgPack015 (1366-1378) and the suppress return (1383) are not modified. If the reporter's case was not duplicate or mixed keys, the reported bug is still present.
findings.suggestion: Get the reporter's actual repro, or diff analyzer output between 3.1.0 and 3.1.1 for a suppressed type, and add that exact input as the regression test. State in the PR which tests fail on base; the per-hunk ablation should confirm which ones do.

findings.title: Field with [Key(null)] as first keyed member still throws ArgumentNullException
findings.body:
The PR aims to stop the analyzer throwing on invalid keys, but one throwing path remains in the field loop. When the first keyed member is a field whose key is neither int nor string, `searchFirst` sets isIntKey to false, the new `continue` is not reached, and the unconditional `else` branch calls `stringMembers.ContainsKey(null)`. The property loop avoids this with `else if (stringKey is not null)`; the field loop has no such guard. This existed before the PR, but it is the same crash class in the lines the PR edits.

Note: the skeptic judged this defect to pre-date this PR.
findings.scenario: `[MessagePackObject] public class Foo { [Key(null)] public string F; }` (with or without SuppressSourceGeneration): MsgPack005 BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull is reported, then ContainsKey(null) throws, giving AD0001 in the analyzer and a generator failure.
findings.suggestion: Mirror the property loop by using `else if (stringKey is not null)` in the field loop, or `continue` right after reporting BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull. Add a field-based [Key(null)] test.

findings.title: Skipping invalid-key members hides MsgPack003 and can add a constructor diagnostic
findings.body: The new `continue` on a key-kind mismatch also skips the recursive `CollectCore(item.Type, item)` for that member, so its type is no longer validated. Duplicate-key members are handled differently: they are dropped from the dictionary but still recursed into. In both cases the member is missing from intMembers/stringMembers when constructor matching runs, so a constructor that takes that member no longer matches. In the source-generator path (reportDiagnostic is null) a formatter is now emitted that silently omits the member, where previously the generator threw.
findings.scenario: `[Key(0)] public string A {get;set;}` and `[Key("b")] public Other B {get;set;}`, where Other is not a MessagePackObject: only MsgPack005 is reported, and MsgPack003 for Other appears only after the key is fixed. Separately, `[Key(0)] A`, `[Key(0)] B` with a sole constructor `Foo(string a, string b)`: MsgPack005 plus a NoDeserializingConstructor diagnostic, because parameter index 1 has no member.

refs.quote: continue; // The key kind does not match the other members; the diagnostic is reported, so skip this member.

findings.suggestion: Either still recurse into the member's type before `continue` so MsgPack003 is reported, or track a `hasInvalidKeys` flag and return null before constructor matching and generation once key diagnostics have been reported. Add tests that combine an invalid key with a non-default constructor.

findings.title: New `continue` on mixed key kinds drops MsgPack003 for that member, also on normal types
findings.body: The added `continue` skips the rest of the loop body, including the recursive CollectCore(item.Type, item) that reports MsgPack003 for the member's type. For a property with an int key following a string-keyed member, the old code did not throw: the `else if (stringKey is not null)` branch was simply skipped and the member type was still collected. That input now loses a diagnostic it used to get, and this is not limited to SuppressSourceGeneration types (AC5).
findings.scenario: [MessagePackObject] class Foo { [Key("a")] public string A {get;set;} [Key(1)] public Other B {get;set;} } where Other has no [MessagePackObject]. Before: MsgPack005 and MsgPack003 on B. After: only MsgPack005; MsgPack003 appears only once the user fixes the key kind.

refs.quote: continue; // The key kind does not match the other members; the diagnostic is reported, so skip this member.

findings.suggestion: Skip only the dictionary insertion for the mismatched member and let the member-type collection still run, or add a test that pins the new behaviour deliberately.

findings.title: Source generator now emits a formatter that silently omits duplicate-key members
findings.body: GetObjectInfo is shared with MessagePackGenerator, which calls it with reportAnalyzerDiagnostic: null. A duplicate key used to throw inside the generator, so no formatter was produced; now the first member wins and the later one is left out of the generated formatter. MsgPack005 is Error by default, so the build normally fails anyway, but a project that downgrades or suppresses MsgPack005 gets a formatter that drops a member without notice. No generator-side test covers this.
findings.scenario: MsgPack005 set to warning in .editorconfig; a non-suppressed type has two members with [Key(0)]. Before: generator exception, no generated formatter. After: generated formatter serializes only the first member and the second is lost on round-trip.

refs.quote: if (TypeCollector.Collect(s.Left.Right, options, referenceSymbols, reportAnalyzerDiagnostic: null, typeSymbol, ct) is FullModel model)

findings.suggestion: Return null from GetObjectInfo (no formatter) when a duplicate or mixed key was found, after finishing diagnostics, or add a generator test that pins the intended output.

discarded.title: Field-path hunks are untested and a [Key(null)] field still throws
discarded.claimed: Every new test uses properties, so the field-loop changes (F2.H4–H6) are not exercised. In that same loop, a field with [Key(null)] that is the first keyed member sets isIntKey to false and reaches stringMembers.ContainsKey(stringKey!) with a null key, which throws ArgumentNullException. The new `continue` only guards the non-first case, so the 'no analyzer failure' goal of U1/U2 is not met for this input. This throw predates the PR.
discarded.detail: Same defect as "Field with [Key(null)] as first keyed member still throws ArgumentNullException" (raised by the correctness lens); merged.

The suppression handling (the late `return null` at line 1383 and the `suppressSourceGeneration is not true` guards) is untouched, so it is identical before and after this PR. The crash being fixed happens equally without the setting, which the PR's own test DuplicateKeysAreReportedWithoutAnalyzerFailureForGeneratedTypes demonstrates. Four of th
discarded.detail: A skeptic wrote a test for the claimed scenario; it passes on the PR head, so the claimed defect did not occur. I wrote CountersignFinding1, which puts the reviewer's scenario (a SuppressSourceGeneration=true type with [Key(0)], [Key(1)] and one member without [Key]) through MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer and expects MsgPack004. It passes on head, and the diff doesn't touch that path, so the failure the reviewer describes doesn't exist. I didn't run it on base. The PR does fix a real analyzer crash in TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo: on base, after reporting MsgPack005 it still called Dictionary.Add with the duplicate key (ArgumentException), and the mixed-key path didn't skip the member. That plausibly explains 'the analyzer does not work'; I found it by reading, not by a test run on base. The reviewer is right that the fix isn't specific to SuppressSourceGeneration and that some new tests only cover unchanged code, but that's a question of how the PR is linked to REQ-2234, not a correctness defect. Whether the crash is what the issue reported needs a human to check the original issue.

refusals.question: Is the duplicate-key / mixed-key-kind analyzer crash the failure that REQ-2234 reports, so that this PR can be accepted as its fix?
refusals.why: The requirement has no repro and does not say which diagnostics went missing. Deciding that this crash is the reported regression needs information from the reporter or the 3.1.0 to 3.1.1 history, which is not in the repository.

options.label: Yes, the crash is the reported bug
options.consequence: The PR is accepted as the fix for REQ-2234. The SuppressSourceGeneration framing in the tests and README is then partly cosmetic, since the crash also occurs without the setting.
options.implementedWhy: TypeCollector.cs:1023 guards the dictionary Add and 1008 skips mismatched members; no suppression logic is changed.

options.label: No, the bug is about diagnostics missing on a valid-key suppressed type
options.consequence: REQ-2234 remains open. This PR is then a separate robustness fix and the real regression still has to be found.
options.implementedWhy: TypeCollector.cs:1383: the suppression return and its guards are unchanged by the diff.

refusals.context: At PR head the suppression early-out sits after all member, constructor and AllowPrivate diagnostics (line 1383) and is not part of the diff. An existing test, MsgPack00xAnalyzerTests.InitPropertyInitializer, already covers a suppressed type. The fixed crash is an ArgumentException or InvalidOperationException from Dictionary.Add / `intKey!.Value`, and it occurs for any [MessagePackObject] type.

refusals.question: When a non-suppressed type has duplicate or mixed-kind keys, should the source generator still emit a formatter that omits the offending member, or emit nothing for that type?
refusals.why: This is a product-behaviour choice about what generated output accompanies an error diagnostic. Before this PR the generator threw, so there is no prior behaviour to preserve.

options.label: Emit a formatter where the first member wins and the offending member is dropped
options.consequence: The build still fails on MsgPack005 (Error by default). If that diagnostic is suppressed or downgraded, a formatter that silently omits a member ships.
options.implementedWhy: TypeCollector.cs:1023-1026 and 1008: the member is skipped and processing continues to ObjectSerializationInfo.Create.

options.label: Emit no formatter for a type with key errors
options.consequence: No partial formatter can ship. The type falls back to dynamic resolvers or fails at run time under AOT, and GetObjectInfo needs an extra early return.
options.implementedWhy: TypeCollector.cs:1008: only `continue`; there is no return null on key errors.

refusals.context: MsgPack005 is listed as Error in AnalyzerReleases.Unshipped.md. The generator calls TypeCollector.Collect with reportAnalyzerDiagnostic: null (MessagePackGenerator.cs:47), so it reports nothing itself.

refs.quote: continue; // The key kind does not match the other members; the diagnostic is reported, so skip this member.

refusals.question: Should the README commit to MsgPack011, MsgPack016 and MsgPack017 staying silent for SuppressSourceGeneration types while all other rules are reported?
refusals.why: The requirement leaves open which diagnostics should stay suppressed, and AC1 read literally says 'the same diagnostics as without the setting'. Publishing this split in the README makes it a documented contract, which is a product decision.

options.label: Keep the split: 011/016/017 silent, the rest reported
options.consequence: Matches current code and the new README section; AC1 must be read as excluding generation-only rules.
options.implementedWhy: TypeCollector.cs:1383 returns before MsgPack011 at 1407; 989 and 921 gate MsgPack017 and MsgPack016.

options.label: Report every diagnostic exactly as for non-suppressed types
options.consequence: Literal AC1; users who opted out get partial-class and AOT errors that do not apply to dynamic resolvers, and existing tests such as DerivedAttributes_SourceGenerationDisabled would have to change.
options.implementedWhy: TypeCollector.cs:1383 returns before the partial-type check.

options.label: Fix the behaviour but do not document the split in the README
options.consequence: Behaviour unchanged with no public promise; the docs hunk (U5) is dropped from this PR.

- Types are accessible to the resolver ([MsgPack012](doc/analyzers/MsgPack012.md)).

notChecked.what: AC3: parity with diagnostics that version 3.1.0 reported for suppressed types.
notChecked.why: No 3.1.0 analyzer binary or baseline output is available, and no test compares against it. The AC1 suppressed-versus-plain parity test is only a stand-in and could hide differences from 3.1.0.

notChecked.what: Generated formatter output for non-suppressed types with duplicate or mixed keys.
notChecked.why: The generator used to throw on this input and now emits a formatter. Only analyzer tests exist, with no generator snapshot, so the emitted code could be wrong or omit members.

notChecked.what: Force-map mode, structs, records, inherited members and assembly- or resolver-level settings with SuppressSourceGeneration.
notChecked.why: The new tests only use the per-type attribute with explicit [Key] members on classes. Other shapes and settings could behave differently or still crash.

notChecked.what: README claim that MsgPack012 and other listed rules apply to suppressed types, and that dynamic resolvers enforce them.
notChecked.why: No test covers MsgPack012 with SuppressSourceGeneration, and neither FindInaccessibleTypes nor the runtime resolver code was read. The README could overstate what is reported or enforced.

notChecked.what: Need for a 3.1.x backport, and behaviour in Unity or IDE-hosted analyzers.
notChecked.why: Release branching and host-specific analyzer loading are outside what the PR shows. The fix may not reach affected users or may behave differently in those hosts.

recommendation.summary: Acceptable once you have made the decisions below. 3 of 5 acceptance criteria are proven by execution; 6 finding(s) (4 reproduced by running code); 3 decision(s) the AI will not make; you are asked to read 22 of 266 changed lines.
distrustIf: The self-test caught 4 of 6 planted bugs — a real bug of the kind that was missed could be in here too.
AC2, AC3 rest on the author agent’s own tests, not on an independent probe.
3 source hunk(s) can be reverted without any test failing — tests would not notice if that code were wrong.
The requirement is ambiguous (5 open point(s)); we checked the change against our reading of it.
Everything was executed on net8.0 / Linux only.
If you find a defect in a unit we told you to skip or skim, record a spot-check miss: it means a proof we relied on was not enough, and trust in this area drops.

canaries.description: The change from `continue; // The key kind does not match the other members; the diagnostic is reported, so skip this` to `break; // The key kind does not match the other members; the diagnostic is reported, so skip this me` changes behaviour in src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:1008.
canaries.note: Reviewer: “Mixed key kind on a property uses `break`, aborting the whole property loop”
canaries.matchWhy: Finding 0 identifies the `break` replacing `continue` in the property loop after the mixed-key diagnostic. It says this aborts the foreach, so later properties are never analyzed and their diagnostics are lost. That is the planted behaviour.

canaries.description: The change from `if (!intMembers.ContainsKey(member.IntKey))` to `if (intMembers.ContainsKey(member.IntKey))` changes behaviour in src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:1023.
canaries.note: Reviewer: “Inverted ContainsKey guard: int-keyed properties are never added to intMembers”
canaries.matchWhy: The finding identifies the inverted `intMembers.ContainsKey` guard in the property loop, which is the mutation at line 1023. It correctly describes the resulting behaviour: new keys are never added, and Add throws when the key already exists.

canaries.description: The change from `if (!intMembers.ContainsKey(member.IntKey))` to `if (intMembers.ContainsKey(member.IntKey))` changes behaviour in src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:1023.
